body:
Gujarat's renewable energy geography

Gujarat is one of India's important centres for solar and wind energy. Its advantages arise from the combination of strong solar radiation, suitable wind conditions, extensive open terrain, a long Arabian Sea coastline and major industrial electricity demand. The state also has transmission infrastructure, ports and industries that can use renewable electricity directly or convert it into products such as green hydrogen.

The distribution of these resources is not uniform. Solar electricity depends mainly on the sunlight reaching a suitable surface, while wind electricity depends on the speed and consistency of moving air. Therefore, an area suitable for a solar park is not necessarily equally suitable for a wind farm.

Kachchh: Open terrain, solar radiation and wind

Kachchh, in northwestern Gujarat, is particularly important because of its relatively dry climate, extensive open areas and wind resources. The region includes the Great Rann of Kachchh, other saline landscapes, grasslands, settlements, agricultural areas and coastal ecosystems.

Many locations receive strong sunlight for much of the year. Dry conditions and comparatively limited cloud cover outside the monsoon can favour solar electricity generation. Large projects can also benefit from suitable land parcels and shared infrastructure.

Kachchh's coastal and open landscapes provide opportunities for wind generation. Wind turbines work best where the wind resource is strong enough, relatively consistent and accessible to the electricity network. Local measurements remain necessary because wind speed differs with terrain, height and season.

The Khavda renewable energy development in Kachchh illustrates the combination of solar and wind potential. Its widely reported 30 GW figure is a development target, not a statement that 30 GW has already been commissioned.

Saurashtra: Coastal wind and solar opportunities

Saurashtra is the peninsula south of the Gulf of Kachchh. Its coastline and exposed locations offer opportunities for wind generation. Areas associated with wind development include parts of Jamnagar, Devbhumi Dwarka, Porbandar, Rajkot, Amreli and Bhavnagar. The exact suitability of a site depends on measured wind conditions, land availability, environmental restrictions and transmission access.

Saurashtra also receives substantial solar radiation. Consequently, solar plants, wind farms and combined solar-wind projects may operate in the wider region. The presence of ports and industrial centres increases the potential value of renewable electricity.

Why climate and physical geography matter

Solar radiation is the energy received from the Sun. A photovoltaic plant generally produces more electricity when sufficient sunlight reaches its modules. Clouds, dust, shading and high operating temperatures can reduce output. Although a hot and sunny place may have a strong solar resource, excessive module temperature can reduce photovoltaic efficiency.

Wind energy depends on the kinetic energy of moving air. Coastal temperature differences, seasonal weather systems and the southwest monsoon influence wind conditions in Gujarat. A sea breeze is a local wind associated with temperature differences between land and sea; it is not the same as the large-scale monsoon circulation. Neither wind nor solar generation is constant throughout the year.

Resource potential is not the same as usable capacity

A region may have excellent sunlight or wind and still face difficulties in developing a project. Electricity must reach consumers through suitable transmission infrastructure. Land ownership, water availability, ecological sensitivity, distance from roads and substations, and the cost of construction also influence feasibility.

Salt flats and dry landscapes should not automatically be treated as empty or ecologically unimportant. Parts of Kachchh support important wildlife, seasonal wetlands and traditional livelihoods. Resource assessment must therefore be followed by suitable site selection.

Prelims focus

  • Kachchh is important for both solar and wind energy development.
  • Saurashtra is a peninsula with significant coastal wind and solar opportunities.
  • Khavda is located in Kachchh and is associated with large-scale solar-wind development.
  • Solar generation depends on sunlight; wind generation depends on moving air.
  • Trap: High theoretical resource potential does not mean an equal amount of installed or operating electricity capacity.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 30-35; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 82-83; Gujarat Power Corporation Limited, Khavda Hybrid Renewable Energy Park project description, June 2024; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Gujarat State Action Plan on Climate Change 2.0 summary, Climate Stress at a Glance, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Why Gujarat, Kachchh and Saurashtra Are Important for Solar and Wind Energy

body:
How solar photovoltaic electricity is produced

A solar photovoltaic (PV) cell converts sunlight directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect. Many cells form a module, and multiple modules can be connected to produce the required amount of electricity. Solar modules generate direct current, while most electricity networks and common household appliances use alternating current. An inverter converts the direct-current output into alternating current suitable for its intended use.

Photovoltaic electricity is different from solar thermal energy. Solar thermal systems collect solar heat for activities such as heating water. Concentrated solar power systems use mirrors to concentrate sunlight and produce high-temperature heat, which can then be used for electricity generation. These are different technologies even though they use the same primary energy source.

Large solar parks

A solar park is an area developed to accommodate solar power projects with supporting facilities such as roads, land arrangements, grid connectivity and electricity evacuation infrastructure. Several developers may establish projects within a park. A solar park is therefore a development arrangement, not a separate scientific method of producing electricity.

Charanka Solar Park, situated at Charanka village in Santalpur taluka of Patan district, is an important example. It is associated with Gujarat's early large-scale solar park development and the use of common infrastructure for multiple solar developers.

Khavda in Kachchh represents a much larger renewable energy development combining solar and wind. The planned scale is commonly described as 30 GW. The distinction between a proposed capacity, capacity under construction and commissioned capacity is essential. A project target must not be added to installed-capacity statistics as though the entire target were operational.

Large solar parks can generate substantial electricity, but they need suitable land and transmission facilities. Their output also varies with the time of day and weather.

Rooftop solar power

Rooftop solar uses panels installed on the roofs of houses, institutions, commercial buildings and other suitable structures. It generates electricity close to where much of it may be consumed. Rooftop generation can reduce electricity drawn from the distribution network during sunny periods, although the exact savings depend on household consumption, the system's output and the applicable billing rules.

A grid-connected rooftop system can use the distribution network when rooftop generation is insufficient. Where permitted, surplus electricity may be exported to the network and accounted for under the applicable metering arrangement. Net metering is a billing arrangement, not an electricity-storage technology. It offsets electricity exported to the grid against electricity imported from it, measured in kWh. A rooftop system without a suitable battery and backup arrangement does not automatically supply electricity during a grid outage.

The Union Government approved PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana on 29 February 2024 to promote residential rooftop solar. Its central financial assistance is directed towards eligible residential consumers under the relevant scheme conditions. It should not be confused with support intended for large utility-scale solar parks.

Modhera: Solar generation combined with storage

Modhera, in Mehsana district, is associated with an important solar village demonstration. On 9 October 2022, it was declared India's first 24x7 solar-powered village. The project combined ground-mounted solar generation, rooftop solar systems and a battery energy storage system.

The project's design included a 6 MW solar photovoltaic plant and 15 MWh battery storage. These two quantities measure different things: MW describes power capacity, while MWh describes an amount of stored or delivered electrical energy. Batteries help make solar-generated electricity available beyond the hours of sunshine. The project demonstrates integration of generation, storage and electricity distribution; it does not mean solar panels produce electricity at night.

Other solar applications

  • Canal-top solar: Panels are installed above sections of canals. They use space already occupied by canal infrastructure and may reduce evaporation locally, but structural cost, access and maintenance remain important.
  • Floating solar: Panels are mounted on suitable water bodies. The arrangement can reduce direct occupation of land, but its effects on water use and aquatic ecology must be assessed.
  • Solar irrigation pumps: Solar electricity operates pumps for agricultural water supply. The electricity source is renewable, but excessive groundwater extraction remains a separate environmental concern.
  • Off-grid solar: A system supplies a local load without depending on a continuous grid connection. Storage or another backup source may be needed when sunlight is unavailable.

Remember: A solar park, rooftop installation, canal-top system and floating system differ mainly in where and how the equipment is installed. All can use the photovoltaic effect to generate electricity.

Prelims focus

  • Charanka Solar Park is located in Patan district.
  • Khavda renewable energy development is located in Kachchh.
  • Modhera is in Mehsana district and was declared a 24x7 solar-powered village in 2022.
  • Modhera's demonstration combines solar generation with battery storage.
  • PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana was approved in 2024 for residential rooftop solar promotion.
  • Trap: Net metering is not the same as battery storage, and rooftop solar does not automatically provide power during a grid outage.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 14, Sources of Energy; Gujarat Power Corporation Limited, Annual Report 2022-23, Gujarat Solar Park and Modhera Solar Project sections; Press Information Bureau, Modhera declared India's first 24x7 solar-powered village, 9 October 2022; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Guidelines for PM-Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, Central Financial Assistance to Residential Consumers, Background and Scope; Gujarat Power Corporation Limited, Khavda project description, June 2024; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Working principle of wind electricity

Wind is moving air. Its kinetic energy can rotate the blades of a wind turbine, which drives a generator to produce electricity. The main physical distinction from solar PV is that wind generation depends on moving air rather than sunlight.

Wind turbines require an adequate wind resource. Wind speed is not constant, so a wind turbine does not produce its rated electrical output continuously. It can generate electricity at night when sufficient wind is available, but it may produce little or no electricity during calm conditions.

Why Gujarat's coast is important

Gujarat's long Arabian Sea coastline, exposed terrain and seasonal wind patterns create opportunities for wind power. Kachchh and parts of Saurashtra are prominent geographical areas for onshore wind development.

Wind availability can vary between the southwest monsoon and other seasons. Open coastal locations may have different wind conditions from inland locations. Developers must measure wind speeds and evaluate the site rather than assume that every coastal location is suitable.

Onshore and offshore wind

Onshore wind means turbines installed on land. Offshore wind means turbines installed in marine waters, generally on suitable seabed foundations or floating structures. Offshore locations can offer strong wind resources but usually involve more difficult construction, marine transmission and maintenance conditions.

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has identified Gujarat and Tamil Nadu as priority areas for offshore wind resource assessment. Its initial assessment identified 8 potential offshore zones near Gujarat and estimated approximately 36 GW of offshore wind potential in those zones.

The 36 GW estimate is a preliminary resource-potential estimate. It does not mean that Gujarat has 36 GW of operating offshore wind power. Actual development depends on surveys, environmental assessment, marine conditions, economics and transmission arrangements.

Wind power is not tidal power

Wind turbines use the movement of air. Tidal energy uses the movement or height difference of seawater associated mainly with gravitational effects involving the Moon and Sun. Gujarat's Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat are important coastal geographical features, but a wind turbine near either gulf remains a wind-energy installation. Its location beside the sea does not make it a tidal-power plant.

How solar-wind hybrid projects work

A solar-wind hybrid project combines electricity generation from solar and wind technologies. These sources may complement one another because their output patterns are often different.

Solar PV generally generates during daylight. Wind may generate during the day or night, depending on actual wind conditions. In some regions, wind generation is relatively strong during the monsoon, when cloud cover can affect solar production. Combining the sources may therefore make total output less variable than either source alone.

However, hybrid does not mean uninterrupted electricity. Low sunlight and weak wind can occur together. Firm or round-the-clock supply may require electricity storage, another reliable source of electricity, suitable grid arrangements or a combination of these measures.

Wind repowering and site limitations

Wind repowering means replacing or upgrading older wind turbines with more effective equipment at an existing wind-energy location. It can make better use of an established wind resource and supporting infrastructure, subject to the required approvals.

Wind development must consider bird movement, land use, nearby settlements, access roads and transmission lines. Offshore development additionally requires assessment of fisheries, marine habitats, navigation and coastal conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Onshore wind turbines are located on land; offshore turbines are located in marine waters.
  • MNRE's initial estimate for Gujarat's identified offshore wind zones is approximately 36 GW.
  • The offshore estimate concerns potential, not operating capacity.
  • Solar-wind hybrids combine 2 variable renewable energy sources.
  • Repowering involves upgrading or replacing older wind-energy equipment.
  • Trap: Offshore wind and tidal energy are not the same technology.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Mineral and Energy Resources, Wind Energy section, printed p. 83; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 14, Sources of Energy; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Offshore Wind, Identified Offshore Wind Zones for Initial Project Development, consulted 16 November 2026; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Policy and Regulatory Updates, December 2025, Gujarat Integrated Renewable Energy Policy 2025 summary, wind repowering provisions.]
